item.title: Nginx static files and API proxy
item.description: Covers how to set up Nginx to serve the frontend files and forward API requests once the frontend and backend are split.
item.content:encoded:
At first the pages were built on the server with Spring Boot and Thymeleaf, the SSR way. Moving the pages to React split the frontend from the backend, and working out how to connect the two led to Nginx. This post looks at how the frontend and backend are connected, and how Nginx is configured for it.

Single application and split structure

A service built as one Spring Boot app has that one app receive every request. A request to / gets HTML built by the app; a request to /api gets JSON. One container, one address.

Build the frontend separately with React or Vue and things change. Running npm run build on the frontend produces a dist/ folder with index.html plus JS and CSS files. These files cannot receive requests on their own. Something has to serve them to the browser. The backend now handles only the API.

Single application Split structure
Pages The Java app builds and returns HTML Built files. A separate program has to serve them
API The Java app The backend
What runs One thing Two things

That raises two questions. Who serves the frontend files? And how does a /api request from the page reach the backend?

One address, split by path

A browser treats two addresses as the same origin only when the scheme, host and port all match. With the pages on :8080 and the API on :8000 the origins differ. The browser does not hand an API response from a different origin to the page’s JS. The page can read it only if the backend sends back CORS headers (response headers saying requests from other origins are allowed), and passing login cookies takes extra settings too.

To avoid this, put one program in front, collect everything under one address, and split by path.

From the browser’s side there is only one address, so there is no origin problem. The program in front looks at the path, forwards /api to the backend, and answers everything else with the frontend files. A program like this is called a reverse proxy.

Proxies and reverse proxies

A proxy is a program in the middle that receives a request on someone’s behalf, passes it on, and returns the response it gets back. The English word literally means acting on someone’s behalf.

Proxies split into two kinds by which side they sit on.

Proxy (forward proxy) Reverse proxy
Which side The requesting side. In front of the browser The receiving side. In front of the servers
Who knows it exists The browser is configured to use it The browser does not know. It thinks that address is the server
What it hides The requester. Servers see the proxy as the one asking The servers behind it. The browser never learns the backend’s address
Example The proxy a company network routes outbound traffic through Nginx forwarding /api to the backend

Plain “proxy” usually means the first kind, a forward proxy. What Nginx does in this post is act as a reverse proxy. The browser only knows app.example.com and has no idea the frontend files and the backend live separately behind it.

The proxy in setting names means the same thing. Nginx’s proxy_pass and the proxy in Vite’s config are both reverse-proxy settings that forward requests to the backend behind them.

Who does it in each environment

The program acting as the reverse proxy differs between local development and the server.

Serving the frontend files Forwarding /api
Local development The Vite dev server (npm run dev) server.proxy in vite.config.ts
Dev server · production Nginx Nginx’s proxy_pass

You can develop locally without Nginx because the Vite dev server does the same job. The dev server started by npm run dev serves the pages and forwards the paths listed under proxy in its config to the backend.

The backend runs separately, started from the IDE or Gradle. The browser only sees localhost:5173, and the dev server forwards anything starting with /api to localhost:8000.

The dev server is for development only. It includes features that reflect code changes on screen immediately, and it is not meant to be deployed. On a server, Nginx serves the dist/ built by npm run build.

Because the two environments do the same job with different config files, the path rules have to be written in both places. Add /auth to the forwarding rules in vite.config.ts, forget it in the Nginx config, and it works locally but returns 404 on the server.

Building dist

The files Nginx serves are built from the frontend project. This assumes Vite.

npm ci instead of npm install installs the same versions every time. Use it when building on a server or in CI.

A finished build leaves a folder like this.

One index.html and a few bundled JS and CSS files. The string after each file name is derived from the contents, so rebuilding after a code change changes the names.

Build modes and environment variables

If dev and production settings differ, build with a mode. Building with --mode dev reads the .env.dev file.

Values starting with VITE_ are written into the JS files at build time. They are not read while running on the server, so changing one means rebuilding.

That is why it is easier to write the API address as a path only, like /api, rather than putting something like https://api.example.com in an environment variable. With the pages and the API at the same address, a path alone reaches the API, and the same build output works on the dev server and in production.

Deploying dist

Put dist/ in the folder Nginx’s root points to. There are three ways.

Mount as a volume Copy into the image Build inside the image
Build npm run build outside the container npm run build outside the container Inside the Dockerfile
Image The official nginx image as is nginx + dist/ nginx + dist/
Deploying a new version Replace the host’s dist/ folder Build outside, then rebuild the image Rebuild the image
Build environment Can differ per PC or CI Can differ per PC or CI Fixed in the Dockerfile

Mounting as a volume means adding -v /opt/web/dist:/usr/share/nginx/html to docker run. The examples in “Connecting containers” below use this.

Copying into the image just puts a dist/ built elsewhere into the image.

The Dockerfile is short and the image is small. The catch is that the build machine needs Node, and different Node versions on different machines can produce different results.

Building inside the image splits the build and the runtime.

The first stage builds with Node; the second carries over only dist/ and the config. Neither Node nor the source code ends up in the final image. Splitting one Dockerfile into stages like this is called a multi-stage build.

Skip the stages and do both building and serving in a single node image, and Node, node_modules and the source code all stay in the final image, pushing it to hundreds of megabytes. None of that is used on the server.

Nginx configuration

A minimal config that serves the frontend files and forwards /api. With the official image it goes in /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf.

server and location

A server block is the set of settings for one port. The location blocks inside it decide what happens per path.

When a request path matches several locations, the longest match wins. /api/users matches both / and /api/, but the longer /api/ handles it. So / can stand for “everything else” and only the paths that need special handling get their own block.

Static files: root and try_files

root is the folder to look for files in. A request for /logo.png returns /usr/share/nginx/html/logo.png.

Page addresses in a React or Vue app are not files. An address like /history/12 is something the JS in the browser created while changing the screen; there is no such file in dist/. Navigating inside the app works because the JS changes the screen, but refresh at that address and the browser requests /history/12 from the server. Nginx can’t find that file and returns 404. try_files is the setting that returns index.html instead in this case.

try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html tries each in order.

Order Looks for Example: /logo.png Example: /history/12
1 $uri: a file with that name Found → returned Not found
2 $uri/: a folder with that name Not found
3 /index.html Returned → the JS draws the /history/12 screen

API proxy: proxy_pass

proxy_pass forwards the request to the backend. upstream gives the backend address a name. You can also write the address directly, as in proxy_pass http://192.168.0.20:8000;.

Once requests go through Nginx, the client the backend sees is Nginx, not the browser. These four headers carry the original request’s details to the backend.

Header Carries
Host The domain the browser requested
X-Real-IP The browser’s IP
X-Forwarded-For The list of IPs along the way. The first is the browser
X-Forwarded-Proto Whether the browser came in over http or https

The backend reads these when it logs client IPs or builds redirect URLs. Leave them out and every request appears to come from Nginx’s IP.

Whether proxy_pass ends in / changes the path the backend receives. Follow a browser request for /api/users.

Request path Matching location proxy_pass Path the backend receives
/api/users /api/ http://backend; /api/users
/api/users /api/ http://backend/; /users
  • Without the /, the request path is passed along untouched. /api/users goes as is
  • With the /, the /api/ that matched the location is removed and replaced with the / written in proxy_pass. /api/ in /api/users becomes /, giving /users

Which one to use depends on the backend’s controller paths.

If the backend returns 404 while the Nginx log shows the request arriving, look here first.

Connecting containers

With Nginx and the backend in separate containers, the question is what to write as the backend address in the Nginx config.

localhost does not work. Inside a container, localhost is that container itself. There is no backend inside the Nginx container, so the connection is refused.

There are two ways.

Host IP connection

No Docker network needs to be created. Publish the backend’s port on the host with -p, and write the server’s IP and that port in the Nginx config.

Nginx goes out of its container to port 8000 on the server, and that port leads into the backend container. If the backend is on a different server, only the IP changes.

The IP to write is the server’s IP. A container IP like 172.17.0.x shown by docker inspect can change when the container is recreated, so it does not go in the config.

Docker network connection

On the same Docker network, Docker resolves container names to addresses. Create a network and start both containers on it.

Here the backend does not need to publish its port with -p. The browser only goes through Nginx, and Nginx reaches the backend inside the network.

Host IP vs. Docker network

Host IP Docker network
Setup None docker network create
Address in the config 192.168.0.20:8000 backend-app:8000
Publishing the backend port Required Not needed
Backend on another server Works Does not. Same server, same network only
If the server’s IP changes The config has to change No effect

How to run the containers themselves is in the Docker post.

Checking and applying the configuration

After editing the config, check the syntax first, then have Nginx reload it if the check passes. The web in these commands isn’t a command; it is the Nginx container name set earlier with --name web.

Reload while nginx -t is failing and Nginx keeps running on the old config. When a change seems not to take effect, look at nginx -t first.

The official image sends its access and error logs to the container’s output, so docker logs shows them directly.

These are the response codes you will see most.

Code Meaning Where to look first
404 (only on refresh) No file for that page address try_files
404 (from the backend) The backend received a different path The / at the end of proxy_pass
502 Bad Gateway Nginx could not connect to the backend The backend address and port, whether the backend container is running
504 Gateway Timeout The backend did not answer in time How long the backend takes. The default wait is 60 seconds

Configuration and command summary

What you want Command / setting
Folder for the frontend files root /usr/share/nginx/html;
Avoid 404 on refresh try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
Send /api to the backend location /api/ { proxy_pass http://backend; }
Name the backend address upstream backend { server host:port; }
Check syntax nginx -t
Reload the config nginx -s reload
Watch the logs docker logs -f web
Create a shared network docker network create app-net

item.title: Using Spring Data Redis
item.description: Covers Spring Boot's Redis connection settings, using StringRedisTemplate per data type, serialization and concurrent updates.
item.content:encoded:
What Redis is and how to look at it in redis-cli is in the earlier post. This post looks at how to connect to Redis from Spring Boot and work with values per data type.

Dependency and connection settings

If the Redis has a password, set password. Do not write it into the config file as is; take it from an environment variable. Leave it out and the first command fails with NOAUTH; get it wrong and the connection fails with WRONGPASS.

These are the settings you will use most.

Setting Meaning Default
host Redis address localhost
port Port 6379
password Password none
database Database number. Used when several apps share one Redis by number (0–15) 0
timeout How long to wait for a single command’s reply 60 seconds
connect-timeout How long to wait while first establishing a connection 10 seconds

Leave timeout out and it is 60 seconds. If Redis stalls, requests wait that long along with it. A short timeout fails fast when something goes wrong, but a command that legitimately takes a while can also fail partway. Decide by how long the commands your app sends actually take. A bare number like 3000 is read as milliseconds.

In Spring Boot 2.x the setting was spring.redis.host. In 3.x it became spring.data.redis.host. If the old name is still there, the value is not applied and the app tries localhost:6379 and fails.

With the starter on the classpath, a StringRedisTemplate is created for you. Inject it.

opsForXxx and Redis data types

RedisTemplate and opsForXxx() are names Spring Data Redis chose, not Redis. What Redis defines is the commands, such as SET and HSET, and the job of actually sending them belongs to the driver underneath, Lettuce (the Spring Boot default). Spring Data Redis sits on top, handles connections and serialization, and groups the commands by data type into methods.

Method Returns Redis data type
opsForValue() ValueOperations String
opsForHash() HashOperations Hash
opsForList() ListOperations List
opsForSet() SetOperations Set
opsForZSet() ZSetOperations Sorted Set

The first row is the confusing one. What Redis calls the String type, Spring calls Value. The rest share the same names.

Commands that act on a key regardless of its data type, like DEL, EXPIRE and TYPE, sit directly on the template: redis.delete(), redis.expire().

You can call opsForXxx() directly in a method chain. With opsForHash(), though, without a variable to assign to, the generic field and value types can’t be inferred and become Object.

Assign it to a variable once and the types are fixed.

The others, such as opsForValue() and opsForList(), use the template’s types as they are, so calling them in a method chain needs no cast.

Serialization

StringRedisTemplate stores keys and values as plain strings, so redis-cli can find the same key and read the value too.

Inject a plain RedisTemplate and its default is JDK serialization, so keys and values go in as bytes converted from Java objects. In redis-cli the key name shows up like "\xac\xed\x00\x05t\x00\tuser:1000", and outside Java the data can neither be read nor found under the same key.

When you need to store a whole object, serialize it to JSON and store the string. Then redis-cli can read it too.

Stored as a string, the value can be read directly in redis-cli or a GUI tool. You need that when checking whether something like a session went in wrong. A value stored with JDK serialization can only be read through Java code.

String

increment raises a stored number and returns the value after raising it. Counting visits per day looks like this.

A missing key starts from 0. A second argument raises it by that much. The return value is a Long, and Redis stores it as a string.

Calling it on a key that holds something other than a number is an error, for example increment on session:a1b2c3, which holds "user=1000".

Hash

HashOperations<H, HK, HV> takes three type arguments: the key type, the field type and the value type, in that order.

List

For a list of recent items, trim right after pushing.

Set

There are two ways to check membership, and the gap grows with the number of members.

isMember takes about the same time whether there are ten members or a million. A Set goes straight to the value internally instead of walking from the start. With members, a million members means a million values over the network before the search even starts.

Sorted Set

reverseRange returns only the values; reverseRangeWithScores includes the scores. A leaderboard that shows scores uses reverseRangeWithScores.

Expiry

getExpire returns -1 for a key with no expiry and -2 for a key that does not exist.

Setting the expiry together with the value is safer. Call set and then expire separately, and an exception or the process exiting in between leaves a key with no expiry.

What happens to the expiry when you change a value depends on the data type. Overwriting a String with set clears the expiry it had. To keep an expiry, pass it again when you overwrite.

Changing a Hash field with put does not touch the key’s expiry. The expiry time you set stays as it was.

Key lookup

redis.keys() looks like an ordinary method, but it sends the KEYS command as is. KEYS walks every key in the database, not just the ones matching the pattern, and Redis handles no other command while it does. The concepts post said KEYS * is not used in production; adding a pattern like session:* does not narrow what gets walked. The reason is in Single-threaded command processing in the concepts post.

Application code rarely needs to find keys. It knows the ID, so it builds the key and reads it directly. When you need a list, do not search for keys; store the list as well when you store the data. If you need the list of active sessions, it looks like this.

Reading the list means reading sessions:active alone. It does not matter how many other keys the same Redis holds.

One catch: Set members have no expiry. When the session key expires after 30 minutes, its ID is still in sessions:active. Remove IDs whose session key is gone when you read the list, or clean them up periodically.

When you occasionally have to walk the keys, such as checking keys in production or cleaning up old keys in bulk, use scan(). It fetches in small pieces, so Redis keeps serving other commands.

Close the Cursor when you are done so its connection is released.

Concurrent updates

To raise a number, use increment.

increment does the read, the add and the write inside Redis as a single command. Redis handles commands one at a time, so even when several servers call it at once, nothing can slip in between. Read with get and write back with set instead, and two servers can read the same value and each write theirs, losing one increment.

Storing an object as one JSON string, then get, change a field, set, has the same problem. One server overwrites the field another just changed with the old value. For an object whose fields change separately, store it as a Hash and write only that field with opsForHash().put(). The concepts post shows this as a diagram in JSON string and Hash compared.

redis-cli commands and their methods

What you want redis-cli Java
Store a value SET k v opsForValue().set(k, v)
With an expiry SET k v EX 1800 opsForValue().set(k, v, Duration.ofMinutes(30))
Read a value GET k opsForValue().get(k)
Increment a number INCR k opsForValue().increment(k)
Set an object field HSET k f v opsForHash().put(k, f, v)
Read a whole object HGETALL k opsForHash().entries(k)
Append to a list RPUSH k v opsForList().rightPush(k, v)
Slice a list LRANGE k 0 9 opsForList().range(k, 0, 9)
Cap a list’s length LTRIM k 0 9 opsForList().trim(k, 0, 9)
Add to a Set SADD k v opsForSet().add(k, v)
Check membership SISMEMBER k v opsForSet().isMember(k, v)
Add with a score ZADD k 120 v opsForZSet().add(k, v, 120)
Top 10 ZREVRANGE k 0 9 opsForZSet().reverseRange(k, 0, 9)
Set an expiry EXPIRE k 1800 expire(k, Duration.ofMinutes(30))
Time remaining TTL k getExpire(k, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
Delete DEL k delete(k)
Check the data type TYPE k type(k)
Find keys SCAN 0 MATCH k* scan(ScanOptions)

item.title: Connecting to a Redis container and checking its state
item.description: Connecting to a running Redis container, checking its state and looking up keys, and connecting a GUI tool to it.
item.content:encoded:
What Redis is and how its data types work is in the concepts post. This post looks at how to connect to a Redis running in a container and check its state.

Connecting with redis-cli

If you started it with Docker, redis-cli is already inside the container. There is nothing to install.

In place of myapp-redis, enter the container name shown in the rightmost NAMES column of docker ps.

You can also connect in one step, without the shell in between.

The difference: the first way lets you look at config files or run other commands inside the container too; the second connects in one line when you only need to run Redis commands.

Size-reduced images such as slim or alpine may not have bash. Use sh instead.

Once connected, the prompt changes to this.

The front is the address and port you are connected to; commands go after the >. exit leaves.

If a password is set, type AUTH your-password first after connecting. Without it every command comes back with NOAUTH Authentication required.

If the port is published to the host and the host has its own redis-cli, you can skip the container and connect directly with redis-cli -h 192.168.0.10 -p 6379.

Checking memory

When Redis reaches its memory limit (maxmemory), it removes keys according to its memory policy. This is called eviction. Check how much memory is in use right now, and whether any keys have been removed by eviction.

Field Meaning
used_memory_human How much is in use now
maxmemory_human The limit. 0B means there is none
maxmemory_policy How the limit is handled
evicted_keys Keys removed by eviction

If evicted_keys is not 0, keys are already being removed. If the removed keys were sessions, that many users have been logged out.

Key lookup and monitoring

You can also run a single command without opening a session. For a Redis inside a container, put docker exec myapp-redis in front.

To find keys, use --scan instead of KEYS. It fetches in pieces, so other commands don’t wait long.

This finds the keys taking up the most memory.

To watch commands as they go by, use MONITOR. It prints every command, so in production turn it on only briefly.

GUI tools

Once there are many keys, you can check key lists and values in a GUI tool instead of redis-cli. GUI tools show JSON values indented, group keys by colon (:), and let you edit values in place.

Tool Characteristics
Another Redis Desktop Manager Open source, free. Windows, macOS and Linux
RedisInsight The official Redis tool, free. Memory usage analysis, slow command log
DataGrip Paid. In the same window as relational databases. Also included in IntelliJ Ultimate
TablePlus Paid. Relational databases and Redis in one tool
VS Code extensions Look up keys and edit values inside the editor

To see a JSON value indented in the terminal, pipe it through jq.

Take care when connecting a GUI to a production Redis. As the concepts post showed, an order being processed or a session has Redis as its original at that moment, so a mistaken delete has nowhere to be restored from. Keep production and development connections distinct in the list, for example by putting [prod] in the connection name.

Ports and SSH tunnels

A GUI connects from outside the container, so the port has to be published to the host.

If nothing comes back, the container was started without publishing the port. There are two ways to connect. One is the GUI tool’s SSH tunnel feature, which goes through the server. An SSH tunnel uses an SSH connection as a passage, forwarding requests from your PC to an address inside the server. The other is to docker exec into the container and use redis-cli.

0.0.0.0 means it is open on every network interface of the host. Anyone who can reach that host can try to connect, so check whether a password is set as well.

An empty value means there is no password. To open it on one interface only, put an address in front: -p 127.0.0.1:6379:6379 instead of -p 6379:6379.

With an SSH tunnel there are two groups of fields to fill in.

What goes in
Host, Port 127.0.0.1, 6379: the Redis address as the server sees it
SSH Host, Port The server IP, 22
SSH Username Your login on the server
SSH Key, Password Authentication for the server

The Redis address is 127.0.0.1 because it is not your PC’s address but the address as seen from the server you connected to over SSH.

Once connected, check which command the button that loads the key list sends before pressing it. If the tool uses KEYS, Redis handles no other command for as long as it runs when there are many keys. Try it against a development Redis first, and you can use MONITOR from earlier to see which command it sends.

Command summary

What you want Command
Connect from inside the container docker exec -it myapp-redis redis-cli
Check published ports docker port myapp-redis
Memory state redis-cli INFO memory
Keys removed by eviction evicted_keys in redis-cli INFO stats
Number of keys redis-cli DBSIZE
Find keys redis-cli --scan --pattern "session:*"
Find big keys redis-cli --bigkeys
Watch commands redis-cli MONITOR

Using it from Spring is covered in Using Spring Data Redis.

item.title: Redis concepts and data types
item.description: What Redis is and why it is fast, its five data types, and the redis-cli commands that go with them.
item.content:encoded:
This post looks at what Redis is, how it differs from a relational database, and how to use its data types and redis-cli commands.

Redis characteristics

Redis is a store you put a value into under a key and read back by that key. It keeps that data in memory, not on disk.

The name is REmote DIctionary Server. Think of the Map you use inside a program, lifted out of the process so several servers can share it. Connect three servers to the same Redis and all three share the same session.

Most of Redis’s characteristics come from storing data in memory instead of on disk.

Property of in-memory storage Result
No round trip to disk Responses mostly take under a millisecond
Memory is the ceiling How much you can hold is limited by the machine’s RAM
Data is lost when the process exits Keeping anything means configuring a separate write to disk

How it differs from a relational database

Only the points that feel different if you are used to relational databases. First, two terms used in the table.

A buffer pool is the area where a relational database holds pages it read from disk. The original is on disk; memory is a temporary spot for what gets used often.

Persistence is writing what is in memory out to disk. Data in memory is lost when the process exits, so a copy is kept in a file to restore it on restart.

Relational DB Redis
Where data lives On disk. Memory is a buffer pool In memory. Disk is for persistence
Data model Tables, columns, types, constraints Key-value. No schema
How you read SQL, with conditions Direct access by key
Joins Yes No
Transactions Commit and rollback, isolation levels Atomic execution, but no rollback
Capacity ceiling Disk size Memory size

Redis is the mirror image. The original is in memory, and what sits on disk is the copy.

Key-based lookup

This is the largest difference. In a relational database you can store data first and decide the query conditions later.

Redis has nothing like this. To look people up by age, you have to build the list of keys for that condition ahead of time.

So Redis is a store where you decide what you will read and how, then write it in that shape. A relational database runs the other way around, which is why you can put a new condition on data you stored long ago.

There is a KEYS * command that lists every key, but it is not used in production. The reason is right below.

Single-threaded command processing

Redis runs command execution on a single thread. It finishes one and starts the next, in arrival order. (Network I/O is split across threads, but the commands themselves run one at a time.)

This design has advantages and points to watch.

  • Advantages: no lock contention and no context switching, so each command is very fast. Two commands never touch the same key at once, which makes counters and locks simple to build
  • Points to watch: while one slow command runs, every other command waits. Type KEYS * against millions of keys and every other request waits it out

When you do need to walk the keyspace, use SCAN. It comes back in pieces, so other commands don’t wait long.

A relational database handles connections in parallel, so one heavy query does not stop other requests from being handled. In exchange you have locks and isolation levels to think about.

Where it gets used

Use What goes in Data type
Sessions Login state String, Hash
In-flight state An order being processed, a task in progress Hash
Cache Results of a relational query String
Counters View counts, call volume String + INCR
Leaderboards Top N by score Sorted Set
Distributed locks Making sure something runs once String + SET NX

It is the same Redis, but the reason for choosing it differs by use. Any one of the six below is reason enough, and several may apply at once.

Requirement Example use
A disk round trip is too slow Cache, in-flight state
Several servers have to see the same thing Sessions, distributed locks
It has to survive a redeploy or restart Sessions, in-flight state
It has to disappear on its own after a while Sessions, cache
Concurrent changes must not drift apart Counters, distributed locks
A sorted order has to stay maintained Leaderboards

The last line, keeping a sorted order, means this: pull a ranking out of a relational database and you sort on every read. A Sorted Set settles the position on write, so the top ten, or one user’s rank, comes back immediately.

Sharing across servers, surviving a restart and expiring automatically have nothing to do with speed. A Map inside the app process satisfies the first condition, no disk round trip, but not these three. A relational database is the opposite: it fails only the first.

On the other hand, the following data is not a good fit for Redis.

  • Anything you search by condition: without the key you cannot find it
  • Anything you keep for a long time: memory costs more than disk
  • Anything that needs transactions: there is no rollback

Where the original data lives

Example If Redis stops
The original is in the relational DB Cache, leaderboards Read it again and refill
Redis is the original Sessions, in-flight state You lose whatever was in flight

Take an order being processed. From payment until shipping starts, the order’s status exists only in Redis. It reaches the relational database as history after processing ends.

If you are holding things Redis is the original for, persistence and the memory policy have to be decided too. The memory policy (maxmemory-policy) is the setting that decides which keys to remove when memory reaches its limit. With a pure cache you can skip the persistence setting, because the data can be read back from the relational database.

JSON string and Hash compared

There are two ways to put an object into Redis.

The first is to store it as one JSON string.

The second is to store it as a Hash.

Reading the whole thing, there is barely a difference. The difference shows when changing part of it.

Say the order status goes from PAID to SHIPPED. The JSON side takes three steps.

The Hash side takes one.

Two things differ here.

How much moves. The JSON side carries the whole object twice to change one field. Thirty fields means thirty received and thirty sent.

Concurrent changes. This is the one that matters.

On the JSON side, server B overwrote everything based on the old value it had read. B never changed status, and yet A’s SHIPPED is gone.

HSET changes only the field you name. There is no read step, so there is no old value to overwrite with.

In summary:

Usage How to store it
You always read and write the whole thing A JSON string is simpler
You change fields separately Hash
Several servers change the same object Hash

Lists work the same way. A JSON array in a String means a full round trip for every addition; a List makes it one RPUSH.

Connecting with redis-cli

The commands below are entered at the redis-cli prompt. If you are running it as a container, connect like this.

Once connected the prompt becomes 127.0.0.1:6379>. exit leaves. Commands for checking its state and connecting a GUI are in Connecting to a Redis container and checking its state.

Data types

Data type What it is Where it fits
String One value under one key Sessions, cache, counters
Hash Fields and values. One object Reading and changing an object field by field
List An ordered list. Push and pop at either end Recent items, a simple queue
Set A collection with no duplicates. No order Deduplication, intersections
Sorted Set A collection ordered by score Leaderboards, time-ordered lists

String

INCR is not a read, add and write back; Redis does it in one go. That is why several servers can raise the same counter without the value drifting.

Hash

The Java equivalents, such as HashOperations, are in part 3.

List

LPUSH to add and LTRIM 0 9 to cut gives you a list that holds the last ten. Trimming on every write is the convention.

RPUSH on one side and LPOP on the other makes a queue. If you need retries or failure handling, you can use a message queue; RabbitMQ, Kafka and Redis Streams are examples. A List queue loses the message if the process handling it exits partway.

Set

SISMEMBER takes about the same time whether there are ten members or a million. A Set goes straight to the value internally instead of walking from the start. Fetch everything with SMEMBERS and search in the app, and the more members there are, the longer the fetch alone takes.

Sorted Set

Each value goes in with a score, and the collection stays ordered by it.

Put a timestamp in the score and you have a time-ordered list. ZRANGEBYSCORE slices it by period.

Expiry (TTL)

Give a key a lifetime and Redis deletes it for you once the time passes. That lifetime is called the TTL, for Time To Live.

TTL answers one of three ways.
A positive number Seconds remaining
-1 No expiry. It stays forever
-2 No such key. Already gone, or never there

A relational database has nothing like this. You keep an expiry column and clear it with a batch job, or compare timestamps on every read. That is why “it has to disappear on its own after a while” counts as a reason to reach for Redis in Where it gets used above.

Setting the expiry as you write the value is safer. SET followed by a separate EXPIRE leaves a key with no expiry if the process exits in between.

Keys piling up with a TTL of -1 is a common reason memory keeps filling.

Spring integration

Connecting from Spring is covered separately, along with what each of these commands maps to in StringRedisTemplate.

Command summary

What you want Command
Store a value SET k v
With an expiry SET k v EX 1800
Read a value GET k
Increment a number INCR k
Set an object field HSET k f v
Read a whole object HGETALL k
Append to a list RPUSH k v
Slice a list LRANGE k 0 9
Cap a list’s length LTRIM k 0 9
Add to a Set SADD k v
Check membership SISMEMBER k v
Add with a score ZADD k 120 v
Top 10 ZREVRANGE k 0 9
Set an expiry EXPIRE k 1800
Time remaining TTL k
Delete DEL k
Check the data type TYPE k

item.title: Docker concepts and Dockerfiles
item.description: Covers writing a Dockerfile to run a Java jar as a container, building and running it, checking inside the container, and moving the image to another server.
item.content:encoded:
This post looks at how to turn a Java app into a Docker image and run it. The examples are Java. A single executable .jar built with Spring Boot is run as a container.

Docker overview

Docker is a tool that bundles everything an app needs to run, so the app behaves the same on any server. No more gaps from a different Java version or one missing library.

Virtual machines and containers compared

A hypervisor is software that divides one physical server’s resources among several virtual machines. It presents virtual CPU, memory, disk and network devices to each virtual machine. The OS installed in a VM runs the same way it would on real hardware, which is why every VM needs its own OS installed.

VMware ESXi, Proxmox, Hyper-V and KVM are hypervisors. An AWS EC2 instance is a virtual machine running on a hypervisor too. VirtualBox, used to run Linux on a laptop, is the same kind of software.

Docker does not divide hardware. It isolates processes on a Linux kernel that is already running. No OS is installed or booted. They work differently, which does not make them incompatible: running Docker inside a VM is a common arrangement.

Virtual machine Container
What sits underneath A hypervisor The Docker engine
OS A guest OS per app Shares the host kernel
Size Gigabytes Tens to hundreds of megabytes
Startup Minutes Seconds

Containers are light because they share the host kernel instead of booting an OS. Isolation uses two Linux kernel features: namespaces divide what files, network and process list a process can see, and cgroups limit how much CPU and memory it can use.

Images and containers

An image packs everything your app needs to run, such as code, runtime, system tools, libraries and settings, into one bundle. It is read-only, so running it a hundred times never changes what is inside.

A container is the process created by running an image. Stop it and remove it, and the image is still there. You can also start several containers from the one image.

Writing a Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is the instruction file that records what goes into the image and how.

An image is made of layers. A layer holds only the files that changed from the state below it, and the layers stack from the bottom up into one filesystem. Of the Dockerfile instructions, RUN, COPY and ADD, which change files, each create a layer. Instructions that only set configuration, such as ENV and ENTRYPOINT, create no layer and are recorded in the image configuration (metadata).

For a Java app it comes down to four decisions.

  1. Which runtime do I stand on → FROM
  2. Where does the jar go → WORKDIR + COPY
  3. How does it start → ENTRYPOINT
  4. What stays out of the image → .dockerignore

The instructions worth knowing

Instruction What it does
FROM The base image to start from. Written on the first line
ARG A variable for build time only. It does not survive into the image
ENV An environment variable for the container. Also available during the build
WORKDIR The working directory for everything after it. Created if missing
COPY Copies a file from the host into the image
ADD COPY plus archive unpacking and URL downloads. Unless you need those, use COPY
RUN Runs a command during the build (installing packages, compiling)
EXPOSE Documents the port this container uses. It does not actually open it
ENTRYPOINT The command that always runs when the container starts
CMD Default arguments for ENTRYPOINT. On its own, the default command
USER The account that runs everything after it. Without it, everything runs as root

The simplest form

For a jar that is already built. The build happened outside, and Docker only packages it into an image.

The openjdk official image is no longer updated. Java images you can use instead include eclipse-temurin, amazoncorretto and azul/zulu-openjdk; this post uses eclipse-temurin. The -jre suffix means only what is needed to run: no compiler, so it is smaller. If you don’t build inside the image, you can use -jre instead of -jdk.

Points to watch when writing it

  • The two forms of ENTRYPOINT. The exec form, ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"], is the default. No shell in between, so signals go straight to the Java process and the SIGTERM from docker stop reaches your app for a clean shutdown. The catch: variables like ${JAVA_OPTS} are not expanded. If you need them, wrap the command in sh -c and write exec java ... so Java replaces the shell. The first process started in a container becomes PID 1, and the signal from docker stop is sent to PID 1. Without exec, the shell stays as PID 1, and the shell doesn’t pass the signal on to Java. docker stop then waits ten seconds and kills it outright, leaving Exited (137). If stopping a container always takes ten seconds, check this first. When it is killed this way, the app terminates without closing connections or finishing the requests it was handling.
  • Time zones. Official base images are often set to UTC. If log timestamps look hours off, check ENV TZ.
  • ARG and ENV are not the same thing. ARG comes in through docker build --build-arg and disappears when the build ends. ENV is baked into the image and visible inside the container. Put a password there and anyone with the image reads it back out of docker inspect.
  • Put the lines that change most at the bottom. The layer cache is reused from the top of the Dockerfile down to the last unchanged line. With COPY app.jar last, a new jar doesn’t rebuild the layers before it.
  • Add a .dockerignore. Without one, the entire folder is shipped to the daemon as build context. Excluding just .git, build and .gradle cuts that down sharply.
  • A non-root run account. For an image used in production, create a dedicated account and set it as the run account with USER.

Build and run

1) Removing the old container and image

To reuse the same name and tag, remove the old ones first.

If an image can’t be removed, check whether a container using it is still there. Check docker ps -a and remove the container first.

2) Build

Go to the folder holding the Dockerfile.

  • -t myapp:1.0: name and tag. Leave the tag off and you get latest.
  • The trailing .: the build context, meaning the current folder. Easy to forget.
  • --no-cache: ignores the cache and rebuilds the image from scratch. Without the cache the build is slower. Use it when a file changed but the change doesn’t seem to show up in the build.

3) Run and check

-f keeps printing new output. Ctrl+C gets you out; the container keeps running.

4) Accessing the container

When the logs don’t show the cause, run a shell inside the container. You can check that a config file is in place and that a volume is mounted.

exec is short for execute; it runs a command inside a running container.

  • -i keeps stdin open and -t allocates a pseudo-terminal (TTY). A shell needs both. Drop either one and no prompt appears, or your input isn’t passed through.
  • exit when you’re done. The container keeps running.

You can also run a single command and come straight back out. There is no prompt waiting for input, so -it is left off; the output still appears on screen without it. Adding -t where there is no terminal, such as in a script or cron, fails with the input device is not a TTY.

A few things worth knowing.

  • exec only works on a running container. You can’t connect to one whose app exited right after starting. Say docker logs shows FileNotFoundException: /app/config/app.yml, and you want to check inside the container whether the config file is really missing or the volume is mounted correctly. In that case, run a new container from the same image with the same volume, but start a shell instead of the app.

    Without --entrypoint bash, the original ENTRYPOINT starts the Java app again, and it exits again on the error that stopped the first container (the missing config file in this example). With bash instead, the app doesn’t run, so the container stays up and you can check the files and settings inside it. Because of --rm, the container is removed when you exit.

  • Connecting as root on permission errors. If the image sets a different account with USER, you may not be able to read the log files.

  • Changes made inside the container are not kept. If editing a config inside the container fixed the problem, you have confirmed the cause, not fixed it. docker rm removes the change along with the container. Carry the same change back to the mounted host folder or into the image.

A script for docker run

Once the options run past a few lines, typing them every time is hard. Save them in a script file and run that.

Option Meaning
-d Run in the background
--name Container name. Without it Docker assigns a random one
--restart unless-stopped Unless you stopped it yourself, starts again after a server reboot or when the app exits
-p 8080:8080 hostPort:containerPort
-e KEY=VALUE Environment variable. Overrides ENV from the Dockerfile
-v hostPath:containerPath Volume mount
-v /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro Borrow the host’s clock. An alternative to -e TZ
-m 1g Memory limit. The default is no limit. A limit keeps one container from using all of the host’s memory, but the container is terminated if it goes over

Remove a container and everything written inside it goes with it. Anything that has to be kept, such as logs and config, goes on a host folder mounted in. Then the files remain however many times the container is recreated. If your app also writes logs to file (a File Appender in logback or log4j2), mount that path out. Left inside, those logs take up disk until they disappear along with the container.

Moving an image as a tar file

A registry is a store you push images to and pull them from (Docker Hub, an internal Harbor, and so on). For servers that can’t reach the internet or a registry, move the image as a file.

  • docker save exports an image to a file; docker export exports a container’s filesystem. To move an image, use save. A file from export doesn’t include the layers or metadata like ENTRYPOINT, so it can’t be run as is.
  • A tar is a bundle, not compression, so it is bulky. docker save myapp:1.0 | gzip > myapp.tar.gz if size matters.
  • load restores the image only. You still start the container with docker run.

Command summary

To do this Run
Running containers docker ps
Including stopped ones docker ps -a
Stop a container docker stop {name}
Remove a container docker rm {name}
List images docker images
Remove an image docker image rm {imageID}
Build an image docker build -t {name}:{tag} .
Run a container docker run -d --name {name} -p 8080:8080 {image}:{tag}
Follow all logs docker logs -f {name}
Follow the last 100 lines docker logs -f -n 100 {name}
Get a shell inside docker exec -it {name} /bin/bash
Inspect the full config docker inspect {name}
Resource usage docker stats {name}
Image to file docker save -o {file}.tar {image}:{tag}
File to image docker load -i {file}.tar
Clean up what’s unused docker system prune

item.title: SSH connections and file transfer
item.description: How to connect to a server with the ssh built into Windows, save connection details in an SSH client, and move files with scp and sftp.
item.content:encoded:
What a server is and which commands you run inside it are in the terminal post. This post looks at how to connect to a server over SSH and how to move files to and from it.

Terminals and SSH

A terminal is the window where you type commands. SSH is a way to connect to another computer over the network and run commands there, with the traffic encrypted. ssh is the command that connects this way from a terminal.

You don’t need to install a separate program to connect to a server. The terminal and the ssh command that come with Windows are enough.

The SSH client built into Windows

Open PowerShell and type it.

The OpenSSH client has been included since Windows 10 1809. mac and Linux have had it in the default terminal all along. You can start without installing anything.

When a client program can’t connect, first check whether ssh in PowerShell can. If ssh fails too, the problem is the server, the network or the account; if ssh works, check the connection details entered in the program.

SSH client programs

Using an SSH client program instead of the plain ssh command adds the features below.

Feature Description
Saved connections No retyping IPs and usernames as the number of servers grows
Tabs Several servers open in one window
Key management Register private key paths and pick one
File transfer A terminal and SFTP in the same window

Commonly used programs:

Program Characteristics
Termius Saved connections, SFTP file transfer by drag and drop. Windows, mac and Linux, with a free plan
XShell + XFtp Terminal and file transfer are separate programs. Free licence for home and school use
MobaXterm SSH terminal, SFTP file transfer, remote desktop and more in one program. Windows
PuTTY Free. Fewer features, but runs as a single executable without installing
VS Code Remote-SSH Opens server files straight in the editor

Connection fields

Menu names differ by client. The fields do not.

Field What goes in
Host, Address The server’s IP or domain
Port 22, or whatever it was changed to
Username The account to log in as
Password, Key The auth method. With a key, point it at the private key file
Label, Name The name shown in the list

Save it once, and from then on you pick the server from the list and connect.

File transfer

For pushing a jar up to a server or pulling a log down.

SFTP is a file transfer method that uses the SSH connection. OpenSSH servers include SFTP in their default configuration, so if you can connect over SSH, SFTP usually works with no extra setup. There is no separate service to run on the server.

It is not FTP, despite the name. FTP has no encryption, and it needs its own service installed and running on the server.

scp

scp stands for secure copy. It copies files over an SSH connection.

What follows the colon is the path on the server. Leave the colon out and the file is copied within your own PC instead of to the server.

The . at the end means the current folder. It is the destination, so it cannot be left off.

sftp

sftp connects to the server and lets you move files while browsing both sides.

The commands with an l in front act on your own machine; the l stands for local. To check which directory you are in on each side, run pwd (server) and lpwd (your machine).

Comparing transfer methods

Situation Method
Transferring a few files Drag them in the client program’s SFTP view
Transferring from a script scp. It runs as one command, and the exit code tells you whether it succeeded
Transferring large files repeatedly rsync. It compares source and target and sends only what changed
Moving or copying files within the server Connect to the server and run cp or mv. The files don’t pass through your PC, so there is no transfer time

Permission errors

If an uploaded file does not appear, or you cannot delete it, check the permissions of the file and folder first.

scp and sftp write files as the account you connected with. Connect as dev and files only land where dev can write. If the folder is owned by root, you are blocked.

Two ways around it. Upload somewhere writable such as your home directory and move it with sudo mv on the server, or change the folder’s owner to dev up front.

Reading the permission string is covered in accounts and permissions in the terminal post.

Command summary

To do this Run Short for
Connect ssh dev@host secure shell
On another port ssh -p 2222 dev@host port
With a specific key ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_rsa dev@host identity
Upload a file scp file dev@host:/path/ secure copy
Download a file scp dev@host:/path/file . secure copy
A whole folder scp -r dir dev@host:/path/ recursive
Connect and transfer sftp dev@host ssh file transfer protocol
Send only what changed rsync -av dir/ dev@host:/path/ archive, verbose

item.title: Terminal basics and permissions
item.description: Covers the basic commands and permission concepts for connecting to a Linux server over SSH and working with its files and logs.
item.content:encoded:
SSH into a server and you see a line like this:

To type the next command at this line, you need to know where on the server you are and how the files on it are laid out. This post looks at the basic concepts and commands for connecting to a server and finding and handling files on it.

Next to each command name is the English word it comes from. For example, rm is short for remove, and pwd for print working directory.

Servers

A server is a computer that other computers connect to and use over the network. Like a PC it has an OS installed and runs programs, but it usually has no monitor or keyboard attached and is operated remotely from another computer.

SSH connection

A shell is the program that reads the commands you type, runs them, and shows the results. When you type commands in a terminal, you are typing into a shell.

ssh is secure shell, an encrypted shell. The command starts a shell on the server and connects its input and output to your screen over an encrypted connection. Type ls and you get the server’s file list.

There are two ways to prove who you are:

  • Password: you type the account’s password
  • Key: you use a key pair made in advance. The public key is registered on the server and the private key stays on the machine you connect from

Which program you connect with, and how to move files, are covered separately.

SSH sessions and process termination

Connecting over SSH creates a session: one connection from login until disconnect, during which a shell runs. Programs you start from that shell become processes belonging to it.

Close the window, shut the laptop or lose the network, and the session ends. The shell then sends a SIGHUP (hang up) signal to the processes it started, and by default a process that receives it terminates. So when a session ends, the programs started in it end too.

Closing the window while watching logs is fine, because the log file is untouched when tail terminates. This is the case that matters:

So programs that need to keep running are run detached from the session. The Docker post described the -d in docker run -d only as “run in the background”. More precisely it is detached, meaning run separately from the session. A container is a process managed by Docker, so it doesn’t receive the SSH session’s signal and keeps running after you close the SSH window.

Where you are, and paths

Windows Explorer shows the current path in its address bar. In a terminal, the shell keeps track of the directory you are working in (your current location), and there is a separate command that prints that path.

pwd is print working directory.

Prompt structure

The prompt is the line the shell shows in front of the cursor while it waits for a command. Most servers include the current location in the prompt, so you can see it without typing pwd.

Part Value Meaning
Before @ dev The account you logged in as
Between @ and : server The server you are on
After : /opt/myapp Current location
Last character $ $ for a normal account, # for root

A ~ in the position field means your home directory. Typing /home/dev every time gets old, so ~ stands in for it.

Absolute and relative paths

Written as Meaning
/opt/myapp/log An absolute path, written from the top /. Points at the same place wherever you run it
log or ./log A relative path, from where you are. . is the current folder
../config .. is one level up. Go up, then into config
~/notes notes under your home

Scripts are safer with absolute paths, since they have to point at the same place no matter where they are run from.

The directory tree

Most Linux distributions lay out their directories according to a standard called the FHS (Filesystem Hierarchy Standard). So from server to server, directories with the same name hold the same kind of files.

Path What is in it
/home/dev The dev account’s home. You start here when you log in
/etc System configuration files
/var/log Logs. /var is variable: files whose contents keep changing while the system runs
/opt optional. Software installed separately. A common home for apps you built yourself
/usr Software the distribution installed. /usr/bin holds the commands
/tmp Temporary files. Depending on the distribution’s settings, cleared on reboot or after a period of time. Don’t keep files here

/ is the top of the tree; /root is the root account’s home directory. Similar names, different places.

pwd, ls, cd

Command Short for
ls list
cd change directory

ls is usually run with options, and the options are abbreviations too.

cd has a few short forms for moving without writing out the full path.

Tab and the arrow keys

Two keys that never make it into a command list but get used constantly.

Tab completes a path from a partial one. Press it twice when several things match and you get the list.

Up arrow brings back the last command you ran. Keep pressing to walk further back. It is what you reach for when a long command needs one small change.

Creating, copying, moving and deleting files

Command Short for What it does
mkdir make directory Creates a folder
touch touch Its actual job is updating a file’s timestamp. Point it at a file that does not exist and an empty one appears, which is the side effect people use it for
cp copy Copy
mv move Move
rm remove Delete

One mv does both renaming and moving. What identifies a file is its path plus its name. Change the name and it is a rename, change the path and it is a move. Same operation, so one command.

Deleting with rm

rm doesn’t move files to a recycle bin, and it doesn’t ask for confirmation. Press enter and the file is deleted immediately, with no way to undo it.

When a script deletes a path held in a variable, check that the path isn’t empty before deleting.

If the variable name is misspelled or the value is never set, $DIR becomes an empty string and rm -rf $DIR/ can run as rm -rf /. set -u stops the script when an undefined variable is used, and the second line exits before deleting if the value is empty.

Viewing file contents

Command When
cat A short file, all of it
head Just the start
tail Just the end
less A long file, one screen at a time

cat is catenate: it prints several files joined together. Give it one file and you get that one, which is how it came to be used for reading.

cat on a log file sends tens of thousands of lines past the screen. Long files go to less or tail. Inside less the arrow keys scroll, /text searches, and q quits.

vi

For editing a file on a server. vi is short for visual.

vi has three modes. The same key does different things in each, so you need to know which one you are in.

It opens in command mode, where every key is a command and typing inserts nothing. Type a sentence in this state and each character runs as a command.

Starting to type

Key Short for What it does
i insert Start typing at the cursor
a append Start typing after the cursor
o open line Open a blank line below and start typing
Esc Stop typing, back to command mode

Saving and quitting

Press : and a colon appears on the bottom line, where you type the command.

Short for
:w write Save
:q quit Quit
:wq write + quit Save and quit. The one you use most
:q! forced quit Quit without saving. Used to discard your changes and leave

Line editing in command mode

Key Short for What it does
dd delete Cut the line the cursor is on. It goes to the clipboard
yy yank Copy the line the cursor is on
p put Paste below the cursor
P Capital pastes above
u undo Undo the last thing
Ctrl+r redo Redo what you undid

dd is d twice because d is the delete command and a range follows it. Pressing d again makes the range “the current line”. With a number in front, 3dd deletes three lines. yy works the same way.

Not sure which mode you are in? Press Esc twice. You end up in command mode either way.

nano

Run something like crontab -e on an Ubuntu or Debian server and nano opens instead of vi, because nano is the default editor on those distributions.

nano has no modes. It opens ready to type, with a list of shortcuts shown along the bottom.

In ^X Exit along the bottom, ^ means the Ctrl key. ^X is Ctrl+X.
Ctrl+O Save (write Out)
Ctrl+X Quit (eXit)
Ctrl+K Cut a line
Ctrl+U Paste
Ctrl+W Search (Where is)
vi nano
Availability Part of the POSIX standard, so present even on most minimal installs May be missing depending on the distribution
Modes Switches between command, insert and colon modes None
Shortcuts Memorised Shown at the bottom of the screen

Checking logs and searching files

Live log monitoring

  • -f: follow. Keeps reading the end of the file and prints new lines as they are added
  • -n 100: number. Prints the last 100 lines first, then keeps printing lines as they are added
  • Ctrl+C to get out

Container logs use options with the same meaning, as in docker logs -f -n 100.

The same option letter can mean different things in different commands. For example, the f in tail -f is follow, but the f in rm -f is force.

Searching file contents

grep is globally search a regular expression and print.

  • -r: recursive, into subfolders
  • -n: number, which line it was on
  • -i: ignore case
  • --include="*.log": only certain extensions

Piping is common too.

| hands the output of the left command to the right one as input. That line prints only the lines containing ERROR among the last 1000.

Accounts and permissions

Linux has an administrator account, root, that can do anything. With root privileges, even a command that deletes system files is not blocked.

So you normally log in as a regular account and run only the commands that need root privileges as root. This limits the damage a mistake can do. The last character of the prompt tells you whether you are logged in as root.

Editing a file you do not have permission for gives an error like this:

In that case, put sudo in front of the command to run just that command as root. sudo stands for substitute user do, run as another account; if no account is given, it runs as root.

If you stay logged in as root, every command runs without restriction, and nothing stops a mistyped rm -rf. Only the line you prefix with sudo runs as root, and only for that moment; the next command runs as the normal account again.

File permission structure

The first ten characters of ls -l are the permissions.

Position In -rw-r--r-- Meaning
1 - Type. - is a file, d a directory, l a link
2–4 rw- user, the owner
5–7 r-- group, anyone in the same group
8–10 r-- other, everyone else

Permissions come in groups of three.

Letter Short for On a file On a directory
r read Can read the contents Can list what is inside
w write Can change the contents Can create and delete files inside
x execute Can run it Can enter the folder

Read the example above and app.yml can only be changed by its owner dev, with everyone else limited to reading. config is owned by root, so the dev account can go in and look but cannot create files there.

There is a numeric form too: r is 4, w is 2, x is 1, added up per group.

Number Letters Meaning
755 rwxr-xr-x Owner does everything, everyone else reads and runs. Common on executables and folders
644 rw-r--r-- Owner writes, everyone else reads. The permission of a newly created file when umask is 022
600 rw------- Only the owner reads and writes. For files nobody else should see

chmod

chmod stands for change mode. It changes a file’s permissions.

Linux doesn’t decide whether a file can run from its extension; it runs because the execute permission is there. With it, ./docker_run.sh works; without it you hand the file to bash as bash docker_run.sh.

The second line is an SSH private key. If its permissions let other users read it, ssh refuses to use the key.

chown and Docker volumes

chown stands for change owner. It changes a file’s owner.

When an app running as root inside a container writes logs into a mounted host folder, those files come out owned by root on the host too.

You can handle each case with sudo, but running the container as a non-root account avoids the problem. Set the account with USER in the image and the files are owned by that account from the start. This is covered in the image-writing section of the Docker post.

item.title: Blog structure and deployment
item.description: The pieces that make up this blog, built with Astro and Starlight, and how posts are written and published to GitHub Pages.
item.content:encoded:
This blog is written in both Korean and English. This post covers the tools it’s built with and how posts are written and published.

The pieces

What it does
Astro Generates static HTML at build time. Almost no JavaScript is sent to the browser.
Starlight Astro’s official docs theme. Search, table of contents, dark mode and multiple languages are built in.
starlight-blog A plugin that turns the docs theme into a blog. It handles the post list, tags and RSS.
Expressive Code Draws code blocks: colours, the file name bar and the copy button. It ships with Starlight.
giscus Comments under each post, stored in GitHub Discussions on the public repo.
GitHub Pages Where the built site is hosted.

Body text uses Pretendard and code uses JetBrains Mono. Both are installed as packages and deployed with the site, so no external font server is involved.

There were two requirements: write in both Korean and English, and be findable in search.

Starlight already has per-language URLs and a language switcher, so those weren’t built by hand. For search, the built HTML contains tags like these.

hreflang tells search engines that the Korean and English pages are the same post in different languages. Without it, the two pages can be treated as duplicate content. A sitemap is generated at build time as well.

On top of that, the pages are static HTML. This post can be read in full without running any JavaScript. What a search engine downloads is a finished document, not an empty <div>.

This only means the conditions are in place for being found; it doesn’t mean ranking near the top of results. That’s something to check once posts have built up and the site is registered with search engines.

Multilingual structure

Korean posts live at the root and English posts under /en/.

Files with the same name are paired as translations of each other. Switching language while reading a post takes you to the same post in the other language.

When there’s no translation yet, Starlight shows the Korean post in its place. There’s no setting to turn this off, so those pages get noindex, which keeps search engines from indexing Korean text as an English page. Once the translation is published, noindex drops off automatically.

Categories and series

Categories are set with tags. Each post lists its top-level category and subcategory as tags.

In the sidebar, posts are grouped under their top-level category following the tree written in src/categories.ts. Tags that aren’t in the tree collect in an Other group; when a post lands there, its tag needs to be added to the tree in src/categories.ts.

Posts meant to be read in order are grouped as a series in src/series.ts.

Posts in a series get the series list at the top and previous/next part links at the bottom. Only this list changes; the post files themselves don’t.

Post frontmatter

  • description and excerpt are used in different places. description is for search engines and link previews; excerpt is for the cards in the post list. Without an excerpt, the list shows a long stretch of the post’s opening.
  • With separate covers for light and dark mode, the one matching the current theme is shown. For a single image, use one image instead of light and dark.
  • With draft: true, a post shows on the dev server but is left out of the build. An unfinished post can be committed without being published.

Images inside posts come in light and dark pairs too. Draw one SVG in concept/<topic>/src/, put its colours in CSS variables, and write the dark-mode values separately. Running the script produces both the light and dark PNGs.

Deployment

There are two ways to publish to GitHub Pages, depending on whether the source repo can be public. On GitHub’s free plan, GitHub Pages is only available for public repos.

Method Source visibility Repos
Single-repo deploy Public 1
Split-repo deploy Private 2

This blog started with a single repo and moved to a split-repo deploy when the source went private.

Single-repo deploy

The source and the site live in one repo. In the repo’s Settings → Pages → Build and deployment, set the source to GitHub Actions, and put this workflow in .github/workflows/deploy.yml.

withastro/action builds the Astro site and uploads it as a Pages artifact, and actions/deploy-pages publishes that artifact to GitHub Pages. Nothing is committed to a branch, so no deploy key or extra branch is needed. pages: write and id-token: write are the permissions actions/deploy-pages needs to publish.

Split-repo deploy

The source and the published site live in separate repos.

Repo Public Contents
Source repo Private Posts, settings, components and other source
Site repo Public Only the built site (HTML, CSS, images)

The site repo is named <username>.github.io. GitHub Pages serves a repo with that name at https://<username>.github.io.

Pushing to main in the source repo sets this off.

The workflow is a single file, .github/workflows/deploy.yml in the source repo. The peaceiris/actions-gh-pages action pushes the built dist folder to the other repo.

force_orphan: true leaves a single commit with no history on every deploy, since the source history already lives in the source repo.

Pushing to another repo needs permission, so a deploy key is used. A deploy key is an SSH key that works for a single repo.

  1. Generate an SSH key pair.
  2. Add the public key to the site repo under Settings → Deploy keys, with Allow write access turned on.
  3. Add the private key to the source repo under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions, named DEPLOY_KEY.

In the site repo, Settings → Pages → Build and deployment has the source set to Deploy from a branch, branch main, folder / (root). The build already happened in the source repo, so the site repo just serves the files it receives.
